peer_results.rationale: AMD's candidates address product return rights estimation (revenue adjustment accounting) and OECD Pillar Two tax legislation status. Neither topic matches Qualcomm's disclosure regarding OEM licensing negotiations and active IP litigation against Transsion.

AVGO's candidates discuss Singapore tax incentives and a Malaysia tax holiday. These tax-related topics are substantively different from Qualcomm's disclosure on OEM licensing negotiations and IP litigation.

comparisons.peer_topic: Intellectual Property Enforcement and Protection Risks
comparisons.peer_summary: Intel cannot always protect or enforce its IP rights due to litigation uncertainties, geopolitical factors, and compulsory licensing regulations, which may harm its competitive position. The theft of trade secrets and inadequate IP protection for innovations also pose risks to the value of R&D investments.
comparisons.comparison: Both Qualcomm and Intel disclose risks and operational realities related to enforcing intellectual property rights. Qualcomm specifically reports active litigation initiated in fiscal 2024 against Transsion to enforce IP rights against unlicensed products (target), whereas Intel discloses the general risk that it cannot always protect or enforce its IP rights due to litigation uncertainties and geopolitical factors (peer). Both address the enforcement dimension of IP licensing, though Qualcomm cites a specific active legal action while Intel cites broad systemic risks.

sentences.text: While we continue to engage in negotiations toward a comprehensive resolution, we have initiated litigation against Transsion in multiple jurisdictions to enforce our intellectual property rights against certain of its unlicensed products.
We cannot always protect our IP or enforce our IP rights.
Our ability to enforce these rights is subject to general litigation risks, as well as uncertainty as to the enforceability of our IP rights in various countries and other geopolitical factors.

peer_results.rationale: MU's candidates address general tax reform risks and the implementation status of OECD Pillar Two legislation. These are tax compliance topics, not comparable to Qualcomm's discussion of OEM licensing negotiations and IP enforcement litigation.

NVDA's candidates concern US export control licensing requirements for specific products to China and related uncertainty. This regulatory export licensing is distinct from Qualcomm's disclosure regarding commercial OEM license agreements and IP litigation against unlicensed products.
